George
Be n s o n
From the very beginning,
the sound of the guitar
was always in my mind.
From the moment I heard
it, I knew that my life was
going to have something
to do with the guitar. I did
not know I was going to be
a player yet, but I loved the
sound.
                                    68
                           46




 As I grew older, I began to dabble with the guitar, to pick it up and try to pick things out. I would get so far, and
 then I would get stuck. I have found later that this is normal. Everybody goes through that on every instrument.
 To move forward, you have to take in more information, and look at things from different angles or from a dif-
 ferent point of view. So I started asking questions from the people whom I knew that had a certain mastery of the
 instrument.

 In my home town of Pittsburg, Pennsylvania, a lot of traveling groups would come through town and I always went up
 to the guitar player to ask if he could show me something. I was never too ashamed to ask. The George Benson you
 know today is a collection of all those people who took the time to show me what they knew, and the things I could
 hang on to did me a lot of good.

 From guitar books, which I was not a reader, I was more of a picture guy. But the demonstrations in the new books
 really helped a lot to show the correct fingerings for this, that, and the other. They showed how to make chords.
 The chords led me to the harmony, that helped me to become a better single line player.

       Peter Farrell
                                  68
                           46




          Peter Farrell was born in Sao Paulo, Brazil in 1981. Son of the singer Claudia Fier and the
          saxophone player Lino Simão. He began studying music at school very young with an early
          interest in flute & violin.

          Still very young, his mother introduced him to the jazz and classical worlds, giving him the
          opportunity to hear the music of George Benson, Antonio Carlos Jobim, Debussy, Ravel,
          Bach, Dori Caymmi, Toninho Horta, Bill Evans, Herbie Hancock and many others.

          However, just like every teenager, Peter loved rock’n’roll and at the age of 11 he asked his
          mother to take him to a guitar teacher. So he began studying guitar with José Walter, which
          gave him the first basic steps to rock and blues.

                              2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved
the George Benson Method                                                                                    4668




            One year later, the young boy was taken by his aunt Léa Freire and his uncle Sizão Mach-
            ado to a music conservatory called Groove, where he studied classical guitar, music
            theory, and jazz guitar with Leyve Miranda and Luis Cavalcante. In this period Peter
            started going deep into the music of George Benson and Wes Montgomery.

            Also in this period, Peter studied Brazilian music with the extraordinary guitar player Lula
            Galvão, and also piano with the great pianist and arranger Edmundo Cassis, who gave him
            a new vision about harmony.

            After many years of studying day and night, Peter started giving his first lessons and re-
            alized he had a great talent to teach and encourage others. Since then teaching has also
            become his passion.

            It did not take long until musicians all over the world started keeping their eyes on him
            because of his ability, technique and musicality. He was very advanced for an 18 year old
            boy. As a matter of fact, Peter was known in the musical scene as a prodigy since he was 14.

            Sometime later Peter was introduced to his idol and mentor George Benson. The connec-
            tion between them was instantaneous. The great Benson was amazed at Peter’s talent and
            how he had decoded many of his secrets. After a few months of friendship, Peter became
                                    68


            Mr. Benson’s private student and it has continued for the past 15 years.

            During the last six years Peter Farrell and George Benson have been dedicated to this col-
                           46




            lection of method books that they have created together: The George Benson Method.

            Peter Farrell has recorded and played with many great artists all over the world such as Jane
            Monheit, Brian McKnight, Eumir Deodato, Cesar Camargo Mariano, Romero Lubambo,
            Adam Rogers, and Didier Lockwood just to name a few.

How to use this book
Although a big part of this method is exclusively dedicated to the guitar, (because it refers to
chord construction and basic visualization of the guitar fretboard),it was created as a tool for all
instruments of all levels (beginner, intermediate and advanced). However, even if you are an
advanced player, make sure you know start at the beginning of the book, otherwise you will
easily get lost by the end of the book.


This method should be used as a dictionary of ideas and techniques. It's important to understand
that the way we approach the musical concepts, ideas and techniques presented here are unique
and cannot be found elsewhere.


Do not worry about learning everything from every chapter. You can go ahead as soon as you
understand the concepts. But always remember that you can come back to any chapter of any
book in order to learn more about a determined subject you want to study again.


Be careful when trying to learn too much at one time. Music is not about quantity but quality.


George and I have been working for many years on this giant collection of books to give you the
best we can and help those that love the guitar the way we do. We hope this method can open a
                               68


new world that was unknown until now. You have a treasure in your hands. It contains all the
knowledge that George Benson has been teaching me privately over the last 15 years.
                      46




Thanks a lot,


Peter Farrell

                                              Important device:
The patterns and scale visualizations in this book may have different time signatures in order to
help with the organization and visualization. Notice that depending on where and how we play
them on the fretboard, we will have more or less possibilities. Don’t let the time signatures
confuse you. Learn the ideas that you like the most and apply them where you feel they sound
the best. Give more attention to the single lines shown.

                                      2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved
The Secret of the Giant Lines
                                                                                               4668




This is one of the most important chapters of this method. From now on, we will be
building single line ideas connecting all the “tools” we have learned previously, such as
scales, arpeggios, scale arpeggios and other ideas. This concept makes the improvisation
much more interesting and unpredictable. We will call this type of single line melodies:
The Giant Lines. To clarify this idea we can deBine them by two things:

a) It must contain at least two bars using 16th notes.
b) It has to combine at least two different scales
Although we study "The Giant Lines" containing two, three, and sometimes four or more,
bars when we apply them we can stop whenever we need to or want to. The Giant Lines
are just a tool to help us memorize single lines and also study technique and articulation.



Static Giant Lines
Static Giant Lines are the combination of many types of scales and arpeggios played over a
single chord simultaneously. However, we must be cautious when playing over dominant
7th chords because they can be found in 3 different situations. Let’s use D7 as an example:

• 1st Situation: Non Leading Dominant Chords in Tonal Songs
                              68


Non leading dominant 7th chords are those that do not lead to any other chord in a tonal
song. They are usually found over the degrees: II, IV, bVI. In these cases we should not use
any “color” (scale) from its dominant (A7), but a combination of dominant scales. The
                     46




example below can clarify what we are talking about:


 4
 4       Cmaj7                      D7                          Dmi7              G7
          I                         II                          IIm               V7
In this progression of chords we have D7 as the IInd degree of “C”. Therefore we can use a
combination of dominant scales such as: “D” Mixolydian, “D” Lydian Dominant and the “D”
blues scale.
We can also add the “D” dominant diminished or “D” Whole Tone scale as two more “colors”
to improvise with.

     2nd Situation: Dominant Chords in Modal or Modal/Tonal Songs                                4668




     To clarify the second situation where dominant chords appear, let’s use a modal/tonal
     harmony for an example:

     Example 1:

     ||   F#m7    |   %     |      %      |       %       |

     |    D7      |   %     |      %      |       %       |

     |    Ebm7    |   %     |      %      |       %   |

     |    F#m7    |   %     |      %      |       %   ||


     Example 2: (Notice that “sus” chords are also considered as dominant 7th chords)

     ||   Dsus |        %           |         %       |       %   |

     |    Dmaj7   |     %           |         %       |       %   |

     | Am7 D7 | Gmaj7 F7 | Bbmaj7 |                           %   |

     |    Em7     |     %          ||
                                    68


     In the cases above, as the dominant chord is not part of a tonal harmony, we have more
                        46




     freedom to try new combinations of scales, even using notes not belonging to the initial
     chord. We will be using combinations of: “D” Mixolydian, “D” Lydian Dominant, “D” blues,
     “D” dominant diminished, “D” altered, “D” major Phrygian and “D” Whole Tone scale.

     Although we can use all these scale combinations, the last note of the single line should
     belong to the initial chord. Of course we might have some exceptions, but for now let’s
     concentrate on the main concept which is to create tension and resolution over a single
     chord.

     On the following pages there are examples of D7 single lines using many types of “Mlux
     and reMlux”. Choose the ones you like and memorize them. Then analyze them one by one
     to make sure you understand the idea. Also try to build other ideas by yourself based on
     the same concepts we have been learning in this chapter.

     In addition to the many scale combinations we have learned, it is time to go deeper into         4668




     7lux and re7lux over a single dominant 7th chord. However in order to organize and better
     understand the new possibilities, let’s split them into what we will call George Benson
     Chord Transitions. (We will keep D7 as example)


     First GB Chord Transition Idea:
     We can create a very interesting outside effect over a D7 chord by playing small A7 ideas
     using the following scales in the middle of the line.


     • “A” Altered
     • “A” Major Phrygian
     • “A” Dominant Diminished
     • “A” Whole Tone
     • “ Dbmaj7 & Bbm7” Scale Arpeggios → remember that Bbm7 = Eb7(9) = A7(b13)

     Attention: Do not stay on the A7 too long because you will destroy the effect of “7lux and
     re7lux” thus making the line sound wrong. For now just analyze and memorize some of the
     examples given on the following pages. As time goes by you will feel more comfortable
     using these ideas.


     Second GB Chord Transition Idea:
                                  68


     Although the ideas above already give the single lines a stronger effect of “7lux and re7lux”,
     we can add one more tool, which is quite simple but will bring some “new colors” to the
     Giant Lines.
                         46




     The second trick is also to create a cadence V7/ I just like we did before by using D7
     leading to G major. However, this time let’s use the relative minor of G major which is Em.
     Therefore, we can use any “B” dominant 7th scale leading to Em. See below:
     • “B” dominant diminished;
     • “B” altered;
     • “B” major Phrygian and
     • “B” Whole Tone

     Attention : In case you want to create your own D7 ideas based on the possibilities given
     in this chapter, make sure that the ending note from your single line idea is a chord tone
     for D7. Anyway, we have many examples on the following pages to guide you into this new
     world of possibilities.

     3rd Situation: Dominant 7th chord Vamp                                                          4668




     In most instances when we have a dominant 7th chord vamp we will 4ind the two following
     options: (Notice: This will help us organize our thoughts when deciding which option to
     use in each situation). Let’s use D7 as an example:

     Option 1: D7(9)
     Over a D7(9) vamp we can use any idea that we have just previously learned. Let's refresh
     our memory:

     • “D” Mixolydian
     • “D” Lydian Dominant
     • “D” Blues
     • “D” dominant diminished,
     • “D” altered,
     • “D” major Phrygian
     • “D” Whole Tone scale
     Going deeper into “4lux and re4lux” we can introduce some A7 ideas (note: do not stay on
     the A7 lines to long otherwise you might destroy the effect of “Blux and reBlux”). See below:
     • “A” Altered
     • “A” Major Phrygian
     • “A” Dominant diminished
     • “A” Whole Tone
     • Dbmaj7 & Bbm7 Scale Aarpeggios → remember that Bbm7 = Eb7(9) = A7(b13)
                                  68


     Option 2: D7(#9)
     In this case we cannot use any scale containing the major 2nd. Therfore we have :
                         46




     • “D” Altered
     • “D” Dominant Diminished
     • “D” Blues
     In addition to all these scale options over a D7 vamp, we can also go deeper to create “4lux
     and re4lex” by playing some A7 ideas leading to the D7 chord as in option 1. (note: do not
     stay on the A7 lines to long otherwise you might destroy the effect of “Blux and reBlux”).
     However, as this chord is very tense, it allows us to superimpose other ideas creating
     outside lines by using some already known materials such as:
     • Ebm Dorian Ideas → Ebm7(9) = Ab7(13) = D7(#9)
     • Gbmaj7 & Ebm7 Scale Arpeggios → Gbmaj7 = Ebm7(9) = Ab7(13) = D7(#9)
     • Dbmaj7 → (resolution from the cadence Ebm7, Ab7 )
     • Bmaj7 & G#m7 Scale Arpeggios → combination betweenn“D” dom-dim & “D” altered

38                            2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved
Superimposition of Major 7th and Scale Ideas Over D7(#9)                                      4668




Although we use the basic scales (altered, dominant diminished, whole tone and major
Phrygian) over dominant 7th chords leading to major or minor, we can also create what we
call superimposed cadences to improve the type of tension we can have before the ending
chord.

This is a subject that we have already covered in the previous GB Method Books in the
chapter about major 7th lines. If we use D7(#9) as an example, we will have the following
superimposed cadences over it:




Cadence 1: Ebm7, Ab7, Dbmaj7

If we apply the tritone substitution over D7, we will Gind Ab7 which can be another Vth
degree of a cadence. In this case we will have: Ebm7, Ab7 and Dbmaj7. Just like the example
above we can use the three chords independently from one another when playing single
lines over a single D7(#9) chord.

• Ebm7 : Dorian , Melodic Minor & Harmonic Minor Ideas


• Ab7 : Only dominant 7th scales containing the major 13th: Mixolydian, Lydian Dominant
and Dominant Diminished, Dominant bebop.
                             68



• Dbmaj7 : Ionian & Lydian (the #4 over this chord will give an A7 altered Glavor to the D7
                    46




line because the notes from Dbmaj7(#4), except for the perfect 5th , are derived from the
“A7” altered scale).


In addition to these cadences, we must remember that every major chord has a relative
minor chord and vice versa, which will double the harmonic possibilities. Therefore, we
can use the scale arpeggios and suggested scales of the following chords:


• Ebm7 (dorian & Melodic Minor)      → Gbmaj7 (Ionian & Lydian)

• Dbmaj7 (Ionian & Lydian)           → Bbm7 (dorian & Melodic Minor)

                         2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved                39
     Cadence 2: Fm7, Bb7, Ebmaj7                                                                    4668




     The answer for using the chords from this cadence is quite simple. If we analyze the Eb
     major scale we will notice that almost all the notes can Fit over D7(#9). Below is a
     comparison between both scales:
                       ___________________________________________
                        ⎮ Eb major scale ⎮           D7(#9)         ⎮
                        ⎮___________________________________________
                                              ⎮                     ⎮
                        ⎮___________________________________________
                             Eb = Root        ⎮ Eb = Minor 2nd      ⎮
                        ⎮___________________________________________
                             F = Major 2nd    ⎮ F = Minor 3rd       ⎮
                        ⎮___________________________________________
                             G = Major 3rd
                                              ⎮ G = Perfect 4th     ⎮
                        ⎮                     ⎮                     ⎮
                             Ab = Perfect 4th    Ab = Augmented 4th
                         ___________________________________________
                        ⎮                     ⎮                     ⎮
                        ⎮    Bb = Perfect 5th ⎮  Bb = Minor 6th
                         ___________________________________________⎮
                             C = Major 6th       C = Minor 7th
                        ⎮___________________________________________
                                              ⎮                     ⎮
                             D = Major 7th    ⎮ D = Perfect Octave ⎮
                        ⎮___________________________________________
     Just like the example before we can use the three chords independently from one another
     when playing single lines over a single D7(#9) chord. Below are the scale possibilities for
     each:

     • Fm7 : Dorian

     • Bb7 : Mixolydian scale

     • Ebmaj7 : Ionian & Lydian
                                    68


     In addition to these cadences, we must remember that every major chord has a relative
     minor chord and vice versa, which will double the harmonic possibilities. Therefore, we
     can use the scale arpeggios and suggested scales of the following chords:
                         46




     • Fm7 (dorian)                  → Abmaj7 (Lydian)
     • Ebmaj7 (Ionian & Lydian)      → Cm7 (dorian & Melodic Minor)

     We can also Find hidden and non common major 7th and minor 7th superimpositions to
     be played over dominant 7th chords by changing the bass note from some guitar chord
     shapes. For example, if we consider "D" as a dominant diminished chord, we could have
     B/D as one of the chord voicing possibilities. Changing its bass from D to G# we will have a
     G#m7 (relative minor from B major).
     In terms of scales, notice that if we consider Bmaj7 as a lydian chord we would have a
     lydian scale for B and a combination between “D” altered and “D” dominant diminished,
     except for one note (C#). On the next page, see the relation between D7 chord and Bmaj7
     lydian scale notes.

40                              2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved
Bmaj7 & G#m7                                                                                      4668




                     ___________________________________________
                    ⎮     B lydian scale     ⎮       D7(#9)       ⎮
                    ⎮___________________________________________
                                             ⎮                    ⎮
                    ⎮___________________________________________
                          B = Root           ⎮ B = Major 6th      ⎮
                    ⎮___________________________________________
                          C# = Major 2nd     ⎮ C# = Major 7th     ⎮
                    ⎮___________________________________________
                          D# = Major 3rd     ⎮ D# = Minor 2nd     ⎮
                    ⎮     E# = Augmented 4th
                                             ⎮ E# = Augmented 2nd⎮
                    ⎮___________________________________________
                                             ⎮                    ⎮
                    ⎮     F# = Perfect 5th   ⎮ F# = Major 3rd
                     ___________________________________________  ⎮
                          G# = Major  6th      G# = Augmented 4th
                    ⎮___________________________________________
                                             ⎮                    ⎮
                          A# = Major 7th     ⎮ A# = Minor 6th
                    ⎮___________________________________________  ⎮

Note: Notice that the B lydian scale is a combination between "D" dominant diminished
and "D" altered scale except for the major 7th.



Summarizing the New Possibilities of Superimposition
Chords over D7(#9):

• Major 7th chords: Dbmaj7, Ebmaj7, Bmaj7, Gbmaj7, Abmaj7, Bbmaj7

• Minor 7th chords:        Bbm7,         Cm7,         G#m7,        Ebm7,          Fm7,   Gm7
                              68
                     46




Attention:
Without thinking about scales, we can play all the scale arpeggios from every chord shown
above. As time goes by you will become more confortable using the scale possibilities with
all the combinations during your solo.
We would like to suggest that you combine simple harmonic ideas with non common ideas
(outside ideas) to create the effect “Dlux and reDlux”. If you play everything with tension you
will sound as predictable as if you were playing only simple ideas without any tension. The
secret is to balance tension and resolution.

It is important to understand that some of the options shown above might not work
depending on how or where we play them. So the best thing to do is memorize and analyze
some of the options we have given to you in this book.

   The World of

     2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved   53
     Clarifying the Melodic World for Minor Chords
                                                                                                      4668




     We can study Giant Lines for minor & major chords in two different ways. First, we must get
     used to playing over a single chord vamp using many types of superimposed arpeggios,
     scales, and "?lux and re?lux" ideas. The reason we start playing over a single chord before
     moving to many chord changes is so we can become free with using our intuition and
     spontaneity while incorporating many of these melodic combinations. Also the chord
     vamps will help us to start leaving behind some rules and the fear of the unknown.

     It is important to know that the majority of single chord vamps are built in minor keys
     because minor chords accept more melodic options than major chords. However, dominant
     chord vamps are also common and work as well as minor harmonies.

     An important trick when comping over minor chord vamps is to play quartal chord
     voicings because it makes the harmony hybrid, which gives more space for new melodic
     ideas (colors). If you are interested in this type of vibe, this is covered in depth in the GB
     Method harmony books.

     Now let’s come back to talk about melodies. Usually when most people improvise over
     minor chord vamps, the dorian scale seems to be their "holy grail" by the fact that it is a
     modal harmony. However, it might sound predictable, at least if you are not John Coltrane or
     McCoy Tyner. Next we will show you some new ideas on how to be more creative over one
     chord improvisation. Let’s use Dm as an example for the following single line ideas and see
     some harmonic possibilities to use over it.

     • Minor Chord Arpeggios & Scale Arpeggios: Dm7, Am7
                                  68


     • Major Chord Arpeggios & Scale Arpeggios: Cmaj7, Fmaj7
                          46




     • Flux & Re>lux Cadences (outside):

     1) Dm7, G7,            Cmaj7               4) Fm7,             Bb7,       Ebmaj7
     2) Bø,   E7,           Am7                 5) Cm7,             F7,        Bbmaj7
     3) Bbm7, Eb7,         Abmaj7               6) Abm7,            Db7,       Gbmaj7


     Note: It is important to understand that each chord from the shown cadences can be used
     independently from one another. Another important detail is that both dominant 7th chords
     from these cadences should be treated as Lydian and Mixolydian. Always remember that
     every tension should be resolved properly according to the vamp chord.



54                            2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved
Clarifying the Superimposed Major 7th Chord Possibilities over Dm                           4668




The major 7th superimposed chord possibilities come from superimposed cadences that
we can apply melodically over dominant 7th chords leading to their landing chord (major
or minor). Below are the explanations for some possibilities:


1) Explaining the superimposed cadences : Dm7, G7, Cmaj7 & Bø, E7, Am7

When we have a static minor 7th chord vamp, we consider it dorian because the dorian
scale has no avoid note. As we know, the dorian mode can be expressed by the cadence
IIm7/ V7. In the case of Dm for example, we have Dm7 and G7, which resolves to Cmaj7.
The best part of the superimposed cadences is that we can play melodies from each chord
individually and also from the cadence itself, no matter what tension we use over the
dominant 7th chord.

As we can use Cmaj7 as a melodic option over Dm, we can also use Am7 which is the
relative minor of C. However, just like we did with Cmaj7 by using its complete cadence,
we can do the same with Am7. Therefore, we can superimpose melodies derived from the
cadences Dm7/ G7/ Cmaj7 & Bø / E7/ Am7 over Dm. Actually, Bø is a Dm6 chord (in other
words we can treat it as Dm dorian) and E7 is the same chord as G7 if we treat them as
dominant diminished. Also E7 is the Vth degree of the “A” harmonic minor scale which
works with the “A” aeolian scale.

Note: We can use any type of dominant 7th scale when playing these cadences thus
creating a beautiful effect of "Jlux and reJlux" over Dm vamp.
                             68
                    46




2) Explaining the Superimposed Cadence : Bbm7, Eb7, Abmaj7

In addition to the cadences below, when we have a static minor chord, we can play
melodies derived from its natural cadence, which in the case of Dm will be: Eø/ A7/ Dm7
or simply A7/ Dm7.

In order to Jind the major 7th chord superimposition options over A7 leading to Dm, let’s
use some tension notes over A7 to help us make some connections between chords. If we
apply the tritone substitution of A7(b13), we will Jind Eb7(9) which is the Vth degree of
Ab major. Therefore we have found the Jirst hidden cadence: Bbm7/ Eb7(9)/ Abmaj7. As
mentioned before, these three chords are independent from each other, so we can use
melodies from both over A7.



                         2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved              55
     3) Explaining the Superimposed Cadences: Fm7, Bb7, Ebmaj7 & Cm7, F7, Bbmaj7                     4668




     In addition to all the melodic possibilities coming from superimposed cadences over Dm,
     by using the knowledge we have learned from the harmonic regions, we can discover
     other major 7th chords thus creating other candeces. As we know the dominant region
     chords can be replaced by the subdominant region chords. So let’s clarify this concept and
     review the harmonic regions from Dm:

     Root Region Chords       Dominant Region chords               Minor Subdominant Region chords
         Dm, Fmaj7                        A7, C#˚                     Gm7(6), C7, Bbmaj7, Ebmaj7

     As we can see, we have found two more options of major 7th chords that can replace A7
     leading to Dm: They are Ebmaj7 and Bbmaj7. Both are derived from the subdominant
     region of Dm. Therefore we can use its cadences: Fm7, Bb7, Ebmaj7 & Cm7, F7, Bbmaj7.

     4) Explaining the Superimposed Cadences : Ebm7, Ab7, Dbmaj7 & Abm7, Db7, Gbmaj7

     We can also Eind superimposed major 7th chords by using the Minor Subdominant Region
     related to the relative major chord. In the case of Dm the relative major is F. Let’s explore
     the new possibilities:

     Minor Subdominant Region Chords (F major key)
     Bbm7, Bbm6 or Bbm(maj7)
     Eb7, Ebsus9
                                   68


     Dbmaj7, Gbmaj7

     Above we can see two more possibilities of major 7th chords that can replace A7 leading
                          46




     to Dm: Dbmaj7 or Gbmaj7, both are derived from the minor subdominant region of "F"
     major. Therefore we can use its cadences: Ebm7, Ab7, Dbmaj7 & Abm7, Db7, Gbmaj7.

     Attention:
     1) Dm7, G7, Cmaj7                      4) Fm7, Bb7, Ebmaj7
     2) Bø,   E7,   Am7                     5) Cm7,  F7, Bbmaj7
     3) Bbm7, Eb7, Abmaj7                   6) Abm7, Db7, Gbmaj7
     The dominant 7th chords derived from the cadences above can use all the scale
     possibilities leading to their landing chord. However, some of these dominant 7th scales
     might sound better than others. In addition to memorizing some of the next examples, we
     advise you to try some of these new possibilities over a Dm vamp backing track. This will
     help you hear the beautiful colors we have been discussing.


56                             2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved
After 'inding the superimposed cadences that can replace A7 leading to Dm, it is time to
                                                                                               4668




organize them in order to 'ind all the relatives from each major 7th or minor 7th chord.

Resolution Chords:                                  IInd Degree Chords:
• Cmaj7:    relative → Am7                          • Dm7:         relative → Fmaj7
• Abmaj7: relative → Fm7                            • Bbm7:        relative → Dbmaj7
• Ebmaj7: relative → Cm7                            • Fm7:         relative → Abmaj7
• Bbmaj7: relative → Gm7                             • Cm7:        relative → Ebmaj7
• Gbmaj7: relative → Ebm7                            • Abm7:       relative → Cbmaj7 (Bmaj7)




                              Summarizing:
• Major 7th Chords:

Dbmaj7, Ebmaj7, Fmaj7, Gbmaj7, Abmaj7, Bbmaj7, Bmaj7, Cmaj7

(Note: the root of each of these chords forms a Db bebop dominant scale)
                            68


• Minor 7th Chords:
                     46




Bbm7, Cm7, Dm7, Ebm7, Fm7, Gm7, Abm7, Am7

(Note: the root of each of these chords forms a Bb bebop dominant scale)



Attention:
Except for Cmaj7 & Am7, which make “Dm” dorian & Fmaj7 lydian, all the other major 7th
& minor 7th superimposed chords can replace A7 leading to Dm. Remember that when a
determined harmony is not a vamp but a cadence to Dm, the best approach to play over A7
is to combine the major 7th & minor 7th superimposed possibilities with any “A” dominant
scale that can lead to Dm. It will make the tensions more comfortable to the ear even when
we create very tense moments.


                        2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved                  57
     • Augmented Major 7th chords                                                                     4668




     The following augmented major 7th chords will give a beautiful “color” to the following
     single line ideas. Below is the explanation of where they come from and why we can apply
     them over Dm:


     F+maj7 (bIII degree in the key of Dm)

     As this is the relative major chord of Dm, the explanation is quite simple. It is derived from
     the “F” bebop scale where the characteristic note is “C#” (this note makes the Fmaj7
     augmented). We can use this over Static Giant Lines and over Active Giant Lines.


     Db+maj7 (VIIth degree in the key of Dm)

     Actually, this chord will give the motion of A7 altered leading to Dm, because the notes
     contained in Db+maj7 also belong to the A7 altered scale. We can use this over Static Giant
     Lines and over Active Giant Lines.


     Bb+maj7 (bVI degree in the key of Dm)

     Although this chord contains the major 3rd from the key (in this case F# is the major 3rd
     of “D”), it sounds very interesting and can give a beautiful color to the single line ideas if
                                   68


     used with wisdom. The Bb+maj7 arpeggio is derived from “E” Locrian major 2nd [Eø(9)],
     which is the II of Dm. This option is the most challenging to apply because it needs an A7
     after it thus forming the cadence: Eø(9) / A7 / Dm7. We can use it over Static Giant Lines
                          46




     and over Active Giant Lines.

     It's important to understand that in addition to the common arpeggios of these augmented
     major 7th chords, we can use their scale arpeggios and their relative minor chords which
     will be minor major 7ths. See below:

     • F+maj7 + Dm(maj7)

     • Db+maj7 + Bbm(maj7)

     • Bb+maj7 + Gm(maj7)




58                             2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved
• Dominant 7th (Lydian and mixolydian): G7, Eb7, Bb7                                           4668




• Key Cadences:

1) Eø, A7, Dm7                              2) Gm7, C7, Fmaj7
      (Bbmaj7)

See below the scale possibilities for A7 leading to Dm7 and C7 leading to Fmaj7:

-   Dominant Diminished
-   Altered
-   Major Phrygian
-   Whole tone

Note: It is important to understand that each chord from the shown cadences can be used
independently from another in order to create the effect of “ :lux and re:lux” over the main
chord (in this case Dm).

• Blues Scale licks: G7, C7

Note: Be careful with the minor 3rd of each blues scale.

• Pentatonic Scales:

After learning the concept of Static Giant Lines, let's jump into the world of the Active Giant    4668




Lines. In theory, Active Giant Lines are the combination of single line ideas derived from a
major or minor key with single line ideas derived from any dominant chord leading to
them. These type of single lines are very similar to the Static Giant Lines that we have
learned on the previous pages, because they also deal with tension & resolution. However,
Active Giant Lines combine only melodic options that describe the V7/ I cadences. Also we
cannot use any dorian idea in the key because they do not work when we have cadences.
Understand that the dorian ideas can be used when superimposed over the dominant 7th
chords leading to the key.

It is important to understand that the concept behind the Active Giant Lines is the same as
previously learned in the chapter discussing Harmonic Minor Single Line Ideas. But this
time we will be using more combinations of dominant 7th scales and also, the lines will be
much longer.

These single line ideas can be used over any beat from any bar derived from any cadence,
mainly minor cadences. However, some options might not sound perfect. As time goes by
we will not have to think about bars or beats anymore because we will get used to where in
the harmony the lines sound best. Make sure to sing all the single line ideas you memorize,
otherwise you will not internalize them and the process of getting used to the sound will
not happen.

Attention: In order to better understand the concept behind the Active Giant Lines, let’s
use the “Dm” key as an example. Although we can combine melodies derived from Dm7
(key) with melodies derived from its relative major (Fmaj7), the melodic options for their
dominant 7th chords must be treated differently because some options might not work.
                              68


For example, the major 7th superimposed ideas will work better for A7 leading to Dm7.
These options over C7 leading to Fmaj7 might sound too tense or even sometimes incorrect.
                     46




The secret is to know the options that will work almout always:

In a cadence || Gm7 | A7 | Dm7 || (IVm, V7, Im) for example, in theory the best options will be:

• All types of A7 leading to Dm7, such as A7 altered, A7 major phrygian, A7 dominant
 diminished, A7 whole tone. In addition to that we have the superimposed major 7th
 chords such as Abmaj7, Dbmaj7, Bbmaj7, Ebmaj7.

• All types of C7 leading to Fmaj7, such as C7 altered, C7 major phrygian, C7 dominant
 diminished, except C7 whole tone. No major 7th chord superimposition (some lines
 might work but the majority will not sound as good as the ones replacing A7 leading
 to Dm).


                          2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved                    91
     Now let's see another option of a cadence where we have a dominant 7th chord leading to a           4668




     major chord such as : || Asus9 | Dmaj7 || (V7 / Imaj7). In theory we could play:

     • All types of A7 leading to Dmaj7 such as A7 altered, A7 major phrygian, A7 dominant
      diminished, A7 whole tone and so on.

     • All types of F#7 leading to Bm7 (which is the relative of D major) such as F#7 altered,
      F#7 major phrygian, F#7 dominant diminished, except F#7 whole tone.




     Important studying tips:
     Always study the Giant Lines you choose over a backing track, than you can practice their
     melodic displacement options, which means to start them every time from a different beat
     of the bar. You will not change their rhythm, you will only displace them to another beat of
     the bar.



     For example, if we have a 16th note Giant Line starting on the Rirst beat of the bar, we can
     also start it from the second, third or fourth beat of the bar. Doing this gives us late or early
     resolutions. Below we have a simple cadence of two bars.
                                        68



     Dm Cadence:          ||            A7            |                Dm            ||
                          46




     Beats per bar :           1    2       3     4        1        2       3    4



     When we have late resolution we "steal" the Rirst two beats from the Dm7 bar to keep
     playing A7, which means we will have:

     Dm Cadence:         ||                 A7                 |                Dm            ||
     Beats per bar :           1        2        3    4            1        2        3    4
     Melodies:             A7        A7         A7    A7           A7       A7   Dm       Dm




92                                 2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved
When we play early resolutions we anticipate the Dm melody "stealing" the last two beats                           4668




from the A7 bar, which means we will have :

Dm Cadence:         ||                 A7                |                       Dm7                 ||
Beats per bar :          1     2        3       4                1           2         3        4
Melodies:            A7       A7       Dm       Dm           Dm              Dm       Dm        Dm




We can also do the opposite by anticipating the A7 line in the last two beats from the Dm7 bar,
which means we will have :

Dm Cadence:         ||                 A7                    |                   Dm7                 ||
Beats per bar :          1      2           3    4                   1        2        3        4
Melodies:                A7    A7       A7      A7           Dm7 Dm7 A7                         A7




Now if we combine both possibilities we can have “endless” Dm7 lines:

Dm Cadence:         ||                  A7                       |                 Dm7                        ||
                                    68


Beats per bar :          1         2        3        4                   1        2         3             4
Melodies:            Dm7 Dm7 Dm7 Dm7                                 Dm7 Dm7               Dm7 Dm7
                         46




Or we could have “endless” A7 lines over all the sequence of chords, leaving only the last
note as the @inal resolution in Dm7.

Dm Cadence:         ||                 A7                |                    Dm7                   ||
Beats per bar :          1      2           3    4               1           2         3        4
Melodies:                A7     A7      A7      A7               A7          A7       A7    A7

This is not a rule but is something to guide us and show us how we can be creative in using
the improvisation positioning which we have learned before in the previous books.


                              2019 © Jupiter Musical Group Ldt. All Rights Reserved                                93
     Where Should We Apply the Active Giant Lines ?                                                                     4668




     We can apply any single line idea from the next examples over the following cadences.
     Although we can stop these melodic ideas whenever we want to, it is important to
     understand that we must always end the melody on a chord tone. Let’s use the key fo Dm
     as an example. Below are a few options:


     A) One Chord Per Bar                                            B) One Chord Per Bar
        (resolution in the key)                                              (no resolution)

     1) ||      A7          |       Dm7 ||                           1) || Bmaj7 |                 A7     ||

     2) ||     Gm7          |       Dm7 ||                           2) ||      Eø         |       A7     ||

     3) || Bbmaj7 |                 Dm7 ||                           3) || Bbmaj7 |                Am7    ||

     4) ||      C#˚        |        Dm7 ||                           4) ||     Gm7         |       C7     ||

     5) ||     Csus        |    Dm7 ||                               5) ||     Gm7         | Bbmaj7 ||

     6) || Bbmaj7 |                 A7   ||                          6) ||     Gm7         | Am7 (A7) ||

     * Sus chords can replace dominant chords in any option
